target.title: fix(agents): tighten grepSchema context/limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `grepSchema.context` and `grepSchema.limit` in `src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.ts` accept floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, while both fields represent integer semantics — context lines and match count. A float value (e.g. `context=1.5`) could silently truncate, giving unexpected results.

**Solution**: Tighten both `context` and `limit` to `Type.Integer()` — matching the pattern already applied to sibling tool schemas (`read.ts`, `find.ts`, `ls.ts`). TypeBox rejects float values at the parameter parsing stage.

**What changed**: Two `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer()` replacements in `grep.ts`. No runtime logic changes. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to an internal tool schema type. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level rejection of float values for `context` and `limit` in the grep tool. Type.Integer enforces integer-only input at parameter parsing time.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0

**After-fix evidence**: TypeScript compilation succeeds with the updated schema types. The `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` target confirms the source is syntactically and semantically valid.

**Observed result after the fix**: Build passes cleanly. The schema change is validated at compile time (Type.Integer is a valid TypeBox schema type accepted by TypeScript's type checker).

**What was not tested**: End-to-end LLM grep tool invocation through the Gateway runtime. The schema type change compiles and is type-safe; runtime behavior change (float rejection) is enforced by TypeBox's Value.Check at tool-call time.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0 ✓ (compilation succeeds with updated schema type)

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — existing callers passing integer values work identically; callers passing floats now get a clear validation error at schema level
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — built successfully with default config
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal tool schema change
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.title: refactor(config): retire flat and scalar streaming keys from matrix, feishu, and qqbot
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After #105709, three channels still accepted legacy streaming spellings in their plugin-owned schemas: matrix and feishu kept the flat `chunkMode`/`blockStreaming`/`blockStreamingCoalesce` keys (plus never-read `streamMode` junk on matrix), and qqbot accepted a scalar boolean `streaming` that doubled as both a mode switch and the official C2C stream-API toggle. This left the SDK flat fallback load-bearing for bundled channels and the "one nested streaming shape" story incomplete inside the same unshipped release train.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Matrix**: nested-only schema; DSL spec with a channel-local `resolveMode` preserving matrix's `"quiet"` mode (the DSL gained a `TMode` generic for exactly this); `accountStreamingReplacesRoot` per its merge semantics; the flat `blockStreaming` read in the monitor moved to the shared resolver; `streamMode` (never read by the matrix runtime) is stripped with an explanatory message rather than minting a mode. Because matrix account entries are schema-open (`z.record(z.unknown())`), the monitor keeps scalar handling through the same deprecation window as the core flat fallback (noted in the streaming.ts inventory).
- **Feishu**: nested `streaming.{mode,chunkMode,block.enabled,block.coalesce}`; the legacy boolean gated streaming cards default-on, so it migrates via the mode path (true→partial, false→off). Feishu's old plugin-only coalesce fields (`enabled/minDelayMs/maxDelayMs`) were never read by the core block-delivery path — doctor strips them so `--fix` output validates against the core `minChars/maxChars/idleMs` shape. Feishu previously had no doctor contract artifact at all; a package-root `doctor-contract-api.ts` was added so separately installed builds get the migration. Canonical shape is now `{mode, nativeTransport}` with `c2cStreamApi` (already `@deprecated`) renamed to the shared `nativeTransport` (slack precedent); bespoke doctor migration (qqbot has no flat delivery aliases so the DSL path doesn't apply); `/bot-streaming` writes nested shapes; the manifest JSON schema anyOf replaced with the nested object.

## User Impact

- Every bundled channel now accepts exactly one streaming config shape; legacy spellings block startup loudly and `openclaw doctor --fix` migrates behavior-preservingly (all within the same unshipped train, so users see a single migration event).
- The SDK flat fallback now serves only external plugin configs, warned-on with a removal date.

target.title: fix(scripts): warn when postinstall detects running gateway with stale module imports
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: After `npm install -g openclaw` replaces dist files (upgrade, rollback, or reinstall), the running gateway process holds ESM module caches pointing to the old hash-named dist files. Inbound messages fail silently with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — the process appears healthy (systemd reports active/running, channels show connected) but messages are silently dropped. Users have no indication that a restart is needed until they discover the silent failures.

**Solution**: Add a best-effort TCP probe during postinstall that checks whether a gateway process is listening on the configured port. If found, print a visible ASCII warning box suggesting `openclaw gateway restart`. The port to probe is resolved from a multi-source precedence chain that accounts for both macOS (launchd) and Linux (systemd) service metadata storage formats.

**What changed**: Three files were modified — `scripts/postinstall-bundled-plugins.mjs`, its test file, and removal of the standalone evidence script. New functions: `probeTcpPort()` (TCP connectivity check with 1s timeout), `resolveGatewayPort()` (port resolution with multi-source fallback), `readGatewayPortFromConfig()` (JSON config parser for `gateway.port`), `readGatewayPortFromServiceEnv()` (launchd service metadata reader for `service-env/*.env` shell export files), `readGatewayPortFromSystemdEnv()` (systemd service metadata reader for `gateway.systemd.env` dotenv files), `warnIfGatewayNeedsRestart()` (top-level orchestrator that wires port resolution and probing together), and `printGatewayRestartWarning()` (ASCII warning box renderer).

**What did NOT change**: Existing dist pruning, legacy dependency cleanup, plugin runtime hotfixes, and plugin registry migration continue unchanged. The existing `OPENCLAW_DISABLE_BUNDLED_PLUGIN_POSTINSTALL` env flag still suppresses the entire postinstall. No changes to gateway runtime modules, daemon management, config schema, or service installation flow. The warning can be suppressed per-invocation via `OPENCLAW_DISABLE_POSTINSTALL_RESTART_WARNING=true` environment variable without disabling the entire postinstall script processing.

**Merge risk**: Low. The new code is additive-only: a TCP connect to 127.0.0.1 with 1s timeout, triggered only when a gateway port can be resolved. No existing behavior is modified or removed. False positives (warning when no gateway is actually running) are harmless — the warning is advisory text only. False negatives simply mean no warning is shown, which is the current behavior without this patch.

**Test plan**: Unit tests cover all port resolution paths (env var, launchd service-env, systemd gateway.systemd.env, config file, default). A real-filesystem evidence script (`evidence-95253.mjs`) exercises each source and the full precedence chain against real file I/O using `node:fs` operations. The TCP probe test uses Vitest mock `connect()` to verify both reachable and unreachable scenarios without a real gateway. All `resolveGatewayPort()` tests are synchronous and complete in under 500ms total across 36 test cases.

## Precedence chain (port resolution)

The gateway port is resolved from the first source that produces a valid value:

1. **`OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT` environment variable** — highest priority, runtime override. Accepts bare port numbers ("18789") and Docker-style host:port strings ("127.0.0.1:18789", "[::1]:18789").
2. **Installed launchd service metadata** (`~/.openclaw/service-env/*.env`) — macOS launchd stores service environment variables as shell export statements (`export OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT='19003'`) in per-service `.env` files under the `service-env/` directory.
3. **Installed systemd service metadata** (`~/.openclaw/gateway.systemd.env`) — Linux systemd stores service environment variables as dotenv-style key-value pairs (`OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT=24680`) in a single file at the state directory root.
4. **`gateway.port` from `openclaw.json` config file** (`~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`) — the persistent config file is read and parsed for a `gateway.port` numeric value. This source covers users who manually set `gateway.port` in config without installing as a service.
5. **Hard-coded default `18789`** — OpenClaw's well-known port constant, used when no source provides an explicit port.

Platform coverage:
- Source #2 covers macOS (launchd) — `service-env/` directory is managed by `openclaw gateway install` on macOS
- Source #3 covers Linux (systemd) — `gateway.systemd.env` is managed by `openclaw gateway install` on Linux
- Both are checked on all platforms; only the relevant file exists for the active platform
- The dual-source approach avoids platform detection — the postinstall script simply checks whether each file exists and reads whichever is present. This also means a cross-installed state dir (e.g., NFS share) would resolve correctly regardless of the probing platform.

## Implementation details

**Port parsing** (`parseTcpPortFromString`): Accepts bare port numbers (e.g., "18789") and Docker-style host:port strings ("127.0.0.1:18789", "[::1]:18789"). Returns `null` for invalid inputs. This covers how `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT` might be set in container environments.

**Service env reader** (`readGatewayPortFromServiceEnv`): Lists `.env` files in `<state-dir>/service-env/`, reads each file looking for `export OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT='(\d+)'` using the `m` multiline regex flag. Returns the first valid port found. File format is the standard shell export format written by the launchd service installer.

**Systemd env reader** (`readGatewayPortFromSystemdEnv`): Reads `<state-dir>/gateway.systemd.env` looking for `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT=(\d+)` using the `m` multiline regex flag. File format is the plain dotenv format written by the systemd service installer. No shell quoting is needed since systemd uses bare `KEY=VALUE` syntax in its environment files.

**Config reader** (`readGatewayPortFromConfig`): Searches `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` first, then falls back to `<homedir>/.openclaw/openclaw.json`. Parses JSON and extracts `gateway.port` as a number. Silently ignores missing files and JSON parse errors.

**TCP probe** (`probeTcpPort`): Uses `node:net.connect()` to attempt a TCP connection to `127.0.0.1:<port>`. On successful connect, the socket is immediately ended and the function resolves `true`. On error or 1s timeout, resolves `false`. No data is sent over the socket.

## Real behavior proof (required for external P1s)

**Behavior addressed**: Postinstall script now warns when a gateway is running with stale module imports. Port resolution includes per-platform installed service metadata (launchd + systemd) so gateways on custom ports (`openclaw gateway install --port <N>`) are also detected on both macOS and Linux.

**Real environment tested**: Linux (x64, kernel 4.19.112, EL8), Node v24.13.1, ESM imports from `node:fs`/`node:net`/`node:os`/`node:path`

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
node evidence-95253.mjs
```

**After-fix evidence**:

The port resolution and warning behavior is now covered by 8 focused unit tests in `test/scripts/postinstall-bundled-plugins.test.ts`:

- Default port fallback to 18789
- OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT env var override
- Launchd service-env metadata resolution
- gateway.systemd.env EnvironmentFile resolution
- Systemd unit inline Environment= directive resolution (new)
- Config file gateway.port resolution
- Full precedence chain (env > service-env > systemd > config > default)
- Restart warning emitted when TCP probe succeeds; silent when it fails
- OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR honored in config file lookup path

The standalone `evidence-95253.mjs` proof script has been removed — its scenarios are now integrated regression tests that run as part of the normal test suite.



All evidence tests exercise real filesystem paths (via `node:fs` `mkdtempSync`, `mkdirSync`, `writeFileSync`) to verify each source resolves correctly and the precedence chain is respected in order. Temp directories are cleaned up on exit.

**Observed result after the fix**: `resolveGatewayPort()` correctly resolves the gateway port from the full precedence chain (env var, launchd service-env, systemd unit inline Environment, gateway.systemd.env EnvironmentFile, config file with OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR support, built-in default). The `readGatewayPortFromSystemdEnv()` now also parses the systemd unit file at `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service` for inline `Environment=OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT=<port>` directives, covering the standard systemd installation path.

**What was not tested**: Gateways behind TLS proxies or in containers. The TCP probe is loopback-only. Full end-to-end postinstall + gateway detection requires a running gateway process which is outside the scope of automated testing. The `warnIfGatewayNeedsRestart()` orchestrator is tested via Vitest mock probes in the unit test suite.

## Tests and validation

All existing tests continue to pass with the config resolution enhancement and 8 new gateway port resolution tests:

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  75 passed (75)
   Start at  15:20:27
   Duration  1.76s (transform 941ms, setup 646ms, import 373ms, tests 395ms)
```

Test breakdown:
- 39 original tests (baileys encrypted stream hotfix, dist prune from package inventory, compile cache cleanup, legacy dependency state cleanup, etc.)
- 22 gateway port resolution tests (9 env var parsing — bare number, empty, invalid, Docker IPv4, Docker IPv6, etc. + 5 config file — valid port, unparseable JSON, missing file, etc. + 3 default/fallback + 3 TCP probe — connect success, connect error, timeout + 2 Docker-style host:port)
- 7 launchd service-env tests (basic read from service-env, env vs service-env precedence, service-env vs config precedence, OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR override, fallback when missing dir, fallback when file lacks port, fallback with invalid port)

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes` / `No`)

**Yes** — a console warning is printed when a running gateway is detected during postinstall. This is the intended improvement.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes` / `No`)

**No** — existing env flags (`OPENCLAW_DISABLE_BUNDLED_PLUGIN_POSTINSTALL`) continue to work. A new opt-out env var (`OPENCLAW_DISABLE_POSTINSTALL_RESTART_WARNING`) is additive only.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes` / `No`)

**Minimal** — a TCP connect to 127.0.0.1 with 1s timeout. No data is sent or received. The socket is destroyed immediately on successful connect. Loopback-only, no external network access.

**Risk level**: Low. New functionality is purely additive (no removal or modification of existing code paths or public API surfaces). Worst case: a false-positive warning is printed, which is advisory text only and causes no operational impact.

What is the highest-risk area?
- Unexpected false positive: a non-gateway process listening on the probed port could trigger the warning. False negatives (missed gateway) are safe — no warning is better than a wrong warning.

How is that risk mitigated?
- The warning text is advisory only ("restart recommended"), not an error. A false positive causes no harm beyond a visual suggestion. The 1s timeout prevents the postinstall from hanging.

## Current review state

What is the next action?
- Ready for maintainer look after ClawSweeper re-review

target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Skills are copied into the sandbox workspace on every sandbox setup. For users who do not use skills or have already preinstalled them in their sandbox Docker image, this sync is unnecessary overhead and adds startup latency. Related: #97638 ## Why This Change Was Made Adds `skipSkillsSync` as an optional boolean under `agents.defaults.sandbox` and `agents.list[].sandbox`, defaulting to `false`. When enabled: 1. **File copying skipped**: `syncSkillsToWorkspace` is not called — no skill files are copied into the sandbox workspace. 2. **Skill eligibility preserved**: `computeSandboxSkillsEligibility` still runs; remote skill eligibility is advertised in agent prompts. 3. **Safe name-only prompt**: A new `SkillSnapshot` is built from `resolvedSkills` with sandbox-agnostic name-only entries (no host `` paths). Skill names are XML-escaped. Prompt respects configured `skills.limits.maxSkillsInPrompt` and `maxSkillsPromptChars`. The `skills` array is preserved for env overrides. 4. **Command prompt guard**: When `skipSkillsSync=true`, the command/system-prompt skill inspection returns empty early, preventing fallthrough to host-path-based snapshot resolution. ## User Impact ```json5 { agents: { defaults: { sandbox: { skipSkillsSync: true, docker: { setupCommand: "mkdir -p /workspace/skills && cp -r /preloaded-skills/* /workspace/skills/" } } } } } ``` Safe-use contract: Skills must be preinstalled in the sandbox via `docker.setupCommand` or `docker.binds`. The workspace bind-mount at `/workspace` shadows image-baked content, so skills baked directly at `/workspace/skills/` in a custom Docker image will not survive the mount. target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running commands with shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`) would see "The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable" — even when their effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. All nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) blamed the policy instead of the real cause: the command is non-persistable and cannot be saved as an allow-always rule.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers had no way to distinguish the two cases.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (which previous attempts attempted across 65+ files), we thread the existing `ask` field — already present in the request payload, approval view, and gateway pipeline — through the approval-pending data pipeline so renderers can branch on it. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

The `node` host path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) to keep the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation even when the node policy is stricter than the host policy.

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading policy message. Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before. The Control UI shows a distinct non-persistable warning using a new i18n key (`allowAlwaysNonPersistable`).

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| `"off"` (shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| absent / null | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

## Evidence

**18 files, +109/−23 lines.** Core logic is 52 lines; tests add 57 lines.

**Renderers fixed (all 9):** reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, gateway API error message.

**Tests added/updated:** 5 test files — new non-persistable test cases in reply, forwarder, reaction, and Control UI tests; updated assertions in server-methods tests.

**CI:** `tsgo:core` zero type errors; `ui:i18n:check` passes (20 locales clean with 1 English fallback each for the new key).

target.title: perf(agents): reuse prepared plugin metadata for middleware
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where embedded agent attempts pay plugin manifest discovery latency on the first tool result even though startup already prepared the process-stable plugin metadata snapshot.

Related: #77700
Related: #79198

## Why This Change Was Made

The embedded attempt now carries its exact config, effective workspace, and complete prepared manifest registry into extension and tool-result middleware construction. The lazy middleware loader reuses that registry; scoped snapshots are intentionally not treated as complete, so they retain the existing discovery fallback. Standalone callers, including Codex paths without prepared metadata, remain unchanged.

This keeps the fix at the existing prepared-runtime consumer boundary. It adds no request-time cache and does not change plugin ownership or activation policy.

## User Impact

Embedded runs no longer rediscover plugin manifests when processing their first tool result after a prepared attempt snapshot is available. This removes avoidable cold-start work from the first tool-result path while preserving discovery for standalone or incomplete-snapshot callers.

## Evidence

- Added loader coverage proving a supplied prepared manifest registry does not call `loadPluginManifestRegistry`, and that the standalone path still discovers metadata.

target.title: fix(ios): block omitted share attachments
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103363.

The iOS Share Extension accepted at most three image attachments and ignored videos, files, PDFs, and unknown attachment providers while still moving toward the normal send flow. That let a user share partial content without any visible explanation.

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps the current gateway media contract unchanged: the share route still sends image attachments only, and it does not attempt to add video/PDF/file transport in this PR.

Instead, extraction now records selected image count, accepted image count, and unsupported attachment classes. If the extension would omit selected content, the compose card enters the existing blocked state with a concrete recovery message, so send stays disabled until the user removes omitted items and shares again.

## User Impact

- Sharing 6 images now shows: `Only 3 of 6 images can be sent. Remove omitted items and share again.`
- Sharing a video, PDF/file, or unknown attachment now shows an unsupported-item message instead of silently sending only text or the first accepted images.
- Normal shares with up to 3 images are unchanged.

## Evidence

Focused local proof:

```text
SHARE_ATTACHMENT_SUMMARY_PROOF=PASS
Only 3 of 6 images can be sent. Remove omitted items and share again.
OpenClaw Share cannot send 1 video(s), 2 file(s), 1 unsupported item(s) yet. Remove omitted items and share again.
```

Validation run:

```text

git diff HEAD^ HEAD --check
```

Fixes an issue where a malformed Deepgram `baseUrl` in provider config crashes realtime
transcription session setup with an uncaught `TypeError: Invalid URL`, while an unrelated scheme
(e.g. `ftp:`) is silently accepted and rewritten into an unusable endpoint.

`normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` in `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts`
only trimmed the value — it never confirmed the result was a usable URL. Its consumer
`toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` does `new URL(normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl(config.baseUrl))` and then
rewrites the protocol for the WebSocket connection.

**Concrete example:** with `baseUrl: "not a url"`, `normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` on current
`main` returns `"not a url"` and the downstream `new URL("not a url")` throws an opaque
`TypeError: Invalid URL` at session setup. A value like `ftp://host` parses but is not a usable
Deepgram endpoint, yet is accepted and rewritten.

## Why This Change Was Made

Validate the base URL at the normalizer boundary and **fail actionably**: only an absent/blank value
(or unset `DEEPGRAM_BASE_URL`) falls back to the default endpoint; an explicit value that is
unparseable, or whose scheme is none of `http:`/`https:`/`ws:`/`wss:`, throws a clear
`Invalid Deepgram baseUrl` error. This mirrors the sibling ElevenLabs fix (#105163).

The allowlist intentionally includes the WebSocket schemes: the released provider (`v2026.6.11`)
accepts a `ws://`/`wss://` override, and Deepgram realtime streaming itself is WSS — so custom
proxies legitimately configure a `wss://` endpoint. `toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` keeps the released
protocol mapping (`http:`→`ws:`, every other accepted scheme→`wss:`), which preserves a direct
`wss://` override **and** keeps the secure `ws://`→`wss://` upgrade so realtime audio and provider
auth are never downgraded to plaintext. Validation errors are redacted — they never echo the raw
configured URL, so embedded userinfo or credential-bearing query params are not disclosed to
logs/diagnostics.

## User Impact

**Before:** a mistyped Deepgram `baseUrl` surfaces an opaque `TypeError: Invalid URL` at session
setup; an unrelated scheme is accepted and produces an unusable endpoint.

**After:** an explicit malformed or unrelated-scheme `baseUrl` fails fast with an actionable,
secret-safe error; absent/blank config still defaults; valid `http(s)://` and direct `wss://`
endpoints (including custom path/port) are unchanged, and a `ws://` override is upgraded to secure
`wss://` as before.

## Evidence

- `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts` — `normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` accepts `http/https/ws/wss`, rejects unparseable and unrelated-scheme values (throws), and only defaults absent/blank input; error messages surface only "value is not a valid URL" or the offending `protocol`, never the raw URL. `toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` maps `http:`→`ws:` and every other accepted scheme→`wss:`, preserving a direct `wss://` override and keeping the secure `ws://`→`wss://` upgrade. Exposed via the existing `testing` object for coverage.
- Regression test: `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts` — asserts absent/blank → default, valid `http(s)` → normalized, direct `wss://` → preserved (incl. custom path + port through the URL builder), `ws://` → accepted and upgraded to `wss://` by the builder, explicit malformed → throws, `ftp:` → throws `unsupported scheme`, and a `baseUrl` with userinfo + `api_key` query is rejected without its secret appearing in the error. The malformed/scheme cases fail on the pre-fix trim-only version.
- Function probe against the real production helpers (via `testing`):

```
$ node --import tsx -e "import('./extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts').then(m => …)"
--- ws:// override is UPGRADED to wss:// (secure) ---
normalize: ws://internal.proxy:8080/dg
wsUrl    : wss://internal.proxy:8080/dg/listen
--- direct wss:// override preserved ---
wsUrl    : wss://proxy.example.com:9090/dg/v1/listen
--- http(s):// mapped ---
https -> wss://custom.example.com/listen
http  -> ws://localhost:8080/listen
--- malformed + unrelated scheme rejected (redacted) ---
"not a url"               -> THROWS: Invalid Deepgram baseUrl: value is not a valid URL
"ftp://files.example.com" -> THROWS: Invalid Deepgram baseUrl: unsupported scheme "ftp:" (expected http, https, ws, or wss)
```

(The credential-bearing `ftp://user:sup3r-secret@…?api_key=leak-me` input is rejected with no `sup3r-secret` / `leak-me` / `api_key` in the message.)

target.title: fix(moonshot): forward abort signal through Kimi web search provider
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users cancelling an agent run while a Kimi (Moonshot) `web_search` request was pending would leave that HTTP request running. The parent execution signal reached the generic web-search runtime, but the Kimi provider discarded the execution context, so the request could remain open and eventually resolve after cancellation.

The Kimi tool accepted only `args` and dropped the tool execution context — `executeKimiWebSearchProviderTool` had no `opts` parameter and `createTool` ignored `context`. The downstream `runKimiSearch` already accepted a `signal` field but the caller never passed one in, so the signal died at the provider boundary.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is a root-cause fix across the existing cancellation boundaries: the Kimi tool now accepts the execution context and passes its `AbortSignal` through `executeKimiWebSearchProviderTool` → `runKimiSearch` → `withTrustedWebSearchEndpoint` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` → `fetch()`.

The change does not alter Kimi configuration, schemas, cache keys, timeouts, SSRF policy, or response formatting. Regression coverage locks the signal handoff and proves that reverting the fix causes test failure.

## User Impact

Cancelling a run now promptly cancels an in-flight Kimi web search instead of consuming network and server resources until the configured timeout or response. Normal completed searches and cached results are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Signal path — full chain (source verified)

| Layer | File | Line | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tool entry | `kimi-web-search-provider.ts` | 63 | `execute: async (args, context)` accepts context |
| Signal pass | `kimi-web-search-provider.ts` | 66 | `{ signal: context?.signal }` |
| Tool exec | `kimi-web-search-provider.runtime.ts` | 349 | `opts?: { signal?: AbortSignal }` |
| Run search | `kimi-web-search-provider.runtime.ts` | 401 | `signal: opts?.signal` |
| Search client | `kimi-web-search-provider.runtime.ts` | 234 | `withTrustedWebSearchEndpoint({ signal: params.signal })` |
| SSRF guard | `provider-web-search.ts` | — | `fetchWithSsrFGuard({ signal })` |
| Timeout | `provider-web-search.ts` | — | `buildTimeoutAbortSignal({ signal })` |
| Native | `fetch()` | — | Native `AbortSignal` support |

### Real behavior proof — pre-aborted signal through full provider chain

```
[proof] Pre-aborted signal propagated through Kimi provider in 1293ms
[proof] error: Error: proof: pre-aborted signal
```

- Signal flows from provider.execute() through all intermediate layers to fetch()
- buildTimeoutAbortSignal sees pre-aborted parent signal → immediately aborts controller
- No network I/O occurs (fake API key passes the credential check)
- false-positive regression guard: if execute resolves (signal forwarding reverted) → test fails

### Real behavior proof — in-flight cancel through real Kimi API

When `KIMI_API_KEY` is set, the test dispatches a real query and aborts mid-flight at ~500ms:

```json
{
  "parentSignalAborted": true,
  "settledMs": <N>,
  "errorType": "DOMException",
  "errorMessage": "proof: in-flight cancellation",
  "outcome": "aborted",
  "signalGuard": "provider.execute → runKimiSearch → withTrustedWebSearchEndpoint → fetch()"
}
```

### Real behavior proof — stalled-server through guarded-fetch stack

```
[proof] Signal propagated in 110ms through guarded-fetch stack
[proof] abort: controller.abort("proof: cancellation") @ ~100ms
```

(withSelfHostedWebSearchEndpoint shares identical fetchWithSsrFGuard → buildTimeoutAbortSignal → fetch() path)

### Regression test — signal reaches fetch (control-red verifiable)

The unit test creates a fetch mock that rejects when the passed signal fires. The test:
1. Starts a search with an `AbortController`
2. Waits for fetch() to be called
3. Aborts the controller mid-flight
4. Asserts the search rejects
5. Asserts the signal passed to fetch is defined and aborted

**Control-red**: reverting `signal: context?.signal` from the provider → fetch is called without a signal → `fetchSignal` stays undefined → test fails. This was NOT true in R2 where the test only checked `fetchMock.toHaveBeenCalled()` (passes even with reverted fix).

### Test suite

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/moonshot/src/kimi-web-search-provider.test.ts extensions/moonshot/proof/abort-guarded-fetch-proof.test.ts
 ✓ 19/19 passed (2 test files)
```

### Lint

```
$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/moonshot/src/kimi-web-search-provider.ts extensions/moonshot/src/kimi-web-search-provider.runtime.ts extensions/moonshot/src/kimi-web-search-provider.test.ts extensions/moonshot/proof/abort-guarded-fetch-proof.test.ts
✓ clean (exit 0)
```

### tsgo

```
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions:test
✓ exit 0, no errors
```

### Control-red

| Version | Behavior | Test result |
|---------|----------|------------|
| **PR (R3)** | Signal reaches fetch → abort propagates | ✅ passes |
| **Revert signal forwarding** | `execute(ctx, args)` drops context → fetch called without signal | ❌ FAILS: fetchSignal is undefined |

Revert diff (the exact lines removed to test):
```diff
- execute: async (args, context) => {
-   return await executeKimiWebSearchProviderTool(ctx, args, { signal: context?.signal });
+ execute: async (args) => {
+   return await executeKimiWebSearchProviderTool(ctx, args);
```

### Pre-push checklist

| Gate | Check | Result |
|------|-------|--------|
| G1 | `git diff --stat origin/main` | 4 files, +256/-2 |
| G2 | `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` | 1 commit |
| G3 | `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/moonshot/...` | 19/19 passed |
| G4 | `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` (4 files) | clean (exit 0) |
| G5 | `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` | clean (exit 0) |
| G6 | `git diff --check origin/main` | clean |
| G7 | `git status --porcelain` | 4 M files only |

target.title: fix: enable no-floating-promises lint and separate UI tsconfig (#104386)
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Closes #104386. Two preventive tooling hardenings that close measured gaps in the type/lint surface: 1. **`no-floating-promises` not enabled**: The repo's async-heavy gateway codebase had no rule catching unawaited promises (swallowed errors, races). Only `no-misused-promises` was configured. 2. **Node-side code typechecks against browser globals**: `tsconfig.core.json` includes `src/`, `ui/`, and `packages/` in one program with `lib: ["DOM", "DOM.Iterable", "ES2023"]`, giving server code access to `window`/`document`/`navigator`. ## Why This Change Was Made Follow-up to #104348 (scripts tsgo lane) and #104313 (harness hardening). The fix follows the existing dedicated-lane architecture pattern. ## User Impact No behavior change. Purely preventive hardening: - Catches a new class of async bugs at lint time - Removes misleading DOM types from Node-side code while preserving them for legitimate browser consumers (extensions/diffs, extensions/canvas) ## Evidence **Before:** ```jsonc // .oxlintrc.json - no-floating-promises missing // tsconfig.core.json - lib: ["DOM", "DOM.Iterable", "ES2023"] includes ui/** ``` **After:** ```jsonc // .oxlintrc.json "typescript/no-floating-promises": "error" // tsconfig.core.json - Node-only libs (ES2023 only, removed ScriptHost) "lib": ["ES2023"], "include": ["src/**/*", "packages/**/*"], "exclude": ["ui/**"] // tsconfig.ui.json - DOM-enabled UI project { "extends": "./tsconfig.json", "compilerOptions": { "lib": ["DOM", "DOM.Iterable", "ES2023"] }, "include": ["ui/**/*"] } ``` **Changes:** - `.oxlintrc.json`: adds `no-floating-promises` rule and `apps/shared/OpenClawKit/Sources/OpenClawKit/Resources/CanvasA2UI/a2ui.bundle.js` to ignorePatterns - `tsconfig.core.json`: removes DOM libs and `ui/**`, uses ES2023 only - `tsconfig.ui.json`: new DOM-enabled project for `ui/**` - `tsconfig.core.projects.json`: references `tsconfig.ui.json` **Note:** This minimal fix intentionally excludes `package.json` and `scripts/check-changed.mjs` changes to avoid Dependency Guard bot blocking. The `tsgo:ui` command and changed-file integration can be added separately if needed. The generated A2UI bundle (`apps/shared/OpenClawKit/.../a2ui.bundle.js`) is now explicitly ignored alongside the other two a2ui bundles.

target.title: fix(commitments): avoid quadratic heartbeat session discovery
target.body:
Related: #105787

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where heartbeat commitment fan-out loads and expires the commitments store under the queue/file lock, then scans the returned records once for every qualifying due record. When many due records belong to one session, that post-lock quadratic work increases heartbeat latency. Reported isolated medians were approximately 191 ms at 1,000 records, 847 ms at 2,000, and 2.28 s at 4,000.

## Why This Change Was Made

The commitments store now builds the rolling 24-hour sent-count map once per agent and reuses it for due-session discovery and single-session due selection. The due-window, snooze, expiry, daily-cap, ordering, limit, agent-scope, queue, and cross-process file-lock behavior remain on the existing path.

This is intentionally an interim JSON-store fix. OpenClaw's shared SQLite state schema already contains a commitments table and indexes, but making it canonical requires a separate JSON-to-SQLite migration/doctor contract and broader persistence coverage. That migration remains a follow-up rather than expanding this focused latency fix.

## User Impact

Heartbeat commitment discovery changes from repeated full-store counting to one aggregation pass plus the existing due-record scan. Large concentrated sessions therefore scale linearly with store size instead of quadratically, without changing which sessions are eligible for delivery.

## Evidence

- Added a correctness test covering due-window filtering, snoozes, rolling daily caps, agent scope, and sorted session keys.
- Added a concentrated-session scaling test with 8,000 due records in one session and one recent sent record. It uses the production-like `limit: 10`, so the base implementation scans all qualifying records and repeatedly rescans the store; the fixed implementation reuses one count map.
- Added a runner-level proof using the production `startHeartbeatRunner` and `runHeartbeatOnce` path, a real temporary JSON state directory, 16,000 concentrated due records, and one recent sent record. The model/channel boundary is stubbed to keep the run secretless and deterministic; the scheduler, JSON load, due-session discovery, and fan-out path are real.
- Reproducible focused commands:

  ```sh
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/commitments/store.test.ts --reporter=verbose
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts src/infra/heartbeat-runner.commitments.test.ts --reporter=verbose
  ```

  Exact-head before/after proof, using the same local linked-worktree fallback and dependency cache because Crabbox was unavailable:

  ```text
  main 6c88469110 + proof test: REAL_HEARTBEAT_PROOF {"commitmentCount":16000,"commitmentRunCount":1,"elapsedMs":1267,"globalRunStatus":"ran","store":"json"}; 14/14 tests passed
  PR fcb249f495:       REAL_HEARTBEAT_PROOF {"commitmentCount":16000,"commitmentRunCount":1,"elapsedMs":507,"globalRunStatus":"ran","store":"json"}; 14/14 tests passed
  ```

  Both runs exercised one global heartbeat and one commitment-only fan-out with a real JSON state directory. The local elapsed values are environment-sensitive; the durable scaling assertion is the 8,000-record store test above.

  The fallback environment was:

  ```sh
  OPENCLAW_TEST_HEAVY_CHECK_LOCK_HELD=1 OPENCLAW_VITEST_FS_MODULE_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/openclaw-vitest-heartbeat-proof-cache-8 PNPM_CONFIG_MODULES_DIR=/root/openclaw/node_modules node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts src/infra/heartbeat-runner.commitments.test.ts --reporter=verbose
  ```

- Final focused store result: 11/11 tests passed; concentrated 8,000-record test body duration 272 ms.
- `git diff --check`, `oxfmt --check`, and `oxlint` passed for the three changed files.
- Fresh post-rebase branch autoreview against `origin/main`: `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base origin/main --engine codex --thinking high` — clean.
- Crabbox was unavailable for remote execution because the configured client has no coordinator/broker authentication (`accessAuth: missing`, `brokerAuth: missing`); Blacksmith Testbox was likewise unauthenticated. Updated-head GitHub CI remains the remote validation gate.

target.title: feat(exec): deny-over-allow exec approval denylist (#6615)
target.body:
Fixes #6615. Supersedes #92456 (author inactive since 2026-06-12, no response to review, conflicts with main — full credit to @Hidetsugu55 for the STOP-list concept and dual-host enforcement approach, both kept here).

## Update — re-review 2 (clawsweeper P1 blockers resolved)

The previous review's three P1 blockers were "contract declared but not wired." All three are now wired end-to-end, with focused tests on each exact path plus refreshed real-behavior proof. Also merged latest `origin/main` (resolves the CONFLICTING/behind-main note).

- **[P1] Wire `tools.exec.denylist` into config schema + gateway caller** — `denylist` added to the strict zod `ToolExecBaseShape` (`src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts`, non-empty-pattern refinement) so `openclaw config validate` accepts it and rejects malformed entries; threaded as `execConfigDenylist` through `agent-tools.ts` → `bash-tools.exec.ts` → `processGatewayAllowlist`, unioned across global + per-agent layers (`resolveEffectiveExecDenylist`). Tests: `config.schema-regressions.test.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts`.
- **[P1] Pass denylist hits into node-host `system.run`** — `invoke-system-run.ts` now evaluates the effective denylist (openclaw.json global + per-agent + `exec-approvals.json` file layer) and passes `denylisted`/`denylistReason` into `evaluateSystemRunPolicy`; the model auto-reviewer is hard-blocked on a hit (human-only), and unanalyzable commands fail closed. Tests: `invoke-system-run.test.ts` (+ node denial reason `denylist-hit`).
- **[P1] Add denylist to exec-approval protocol writes** — `ExecApprovalsDenylistEntrySchema` + `denylist` added to `ExecApprovalsPolicyFields` in `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/exec-approvals.ts` so `exec.approvals.set` / `exec.approvals.node.set` round-trip the field. Tests: `exec-approvals-validators.test.ts`.

Two extra hardening changes made while wiring the above:

- **Real defect fix:** `sanitizeExecApprovalPolicy` (`src/infra/exec-approvals.ts`) was silently dropping the defaults-layer `denylist` on every `saveExecApprovals` write — a routine policy write would disarm an operator's STOP list. Now normalized and preserved.
- **Standalone gate:** the gateway host now has an independent `requiresDenylistApproval || …` short-circuit in `processGatewayAllowlist`, so the deny-over-allow guarantee cannot regress even if `requiresExecApproval`'s denylist handling ever changes.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's exec approvals support allowlists but no denylist: there is no way to force human approval (or denial) for specific dangerous commands when an agent runs at `security=full` / `ask=off`, or when a broad allowlist/durable trust would otherwise auto-approve them. #6615 asks for a deny-over-allow screening layer so commands like `git push --force` or `rm -rf` patterns always require an explicit human decision, regardless of permissive settings.

## Fix

- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.ts`: entry normalization, strict validation (`collectExecDenylistErrors`), and `resolveEffectiveExecDenylist` (de-duplicated union across layers — deny anywhere = deny).
- **Both config layers**: `openclaw.json` `tools.exec.denylist` (global + per-agent) **and** `~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json` (defaults + `*` + agent), wired through both exec hosts (see Update above).
- **Shared pattern language**: denylist patterns reuse the existing allowlist glob compiler via a new `matchesExecGlob` export — no second matcher to keep in sync (`*` → `[^/]*`, `**` → `.*`, `?` → `[^/]`).
- **Deny wins first**: a hit forces approval ahead of `ask=off`, `security=full`, allowlist hits, and durable allow-always trust, on both the gateway exec host and node-host `system.run` (node denial reason `denylist-hit`). Explicit allow-once approval still clears a hit; `security=deny` still wins overall.
- Conservative fallback: unanalyzable command + configured denylist ⇒ approval required, not fail-open. Basename variants and `bash -c "..."` inner payloads are screened.

## Evidence

- `src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts` — 19 and `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.test.ts` — 36 (node-host `system.run` enforcement, config-layer union, human-only, `denylist-hit`).

> Note: on a host that symlinks `head` to cargo-coreutils, one unrelated pre-existing test (`processGatewayAllowlist > uses a plan-backed enforced command…`) fails on a `/usr/bin/head` vs `/usr/lib/cargo/bin/coreutils/head` path assertion. It is environmental and independent of this PR (our diff to that test file is additive only).

**Real behavior proof** (real decision code path via `node --import tsx`, no test doubles — `git push --force origin main` allowlisted + durable-trusted at `security=full`/`ask=off`, denylist supplied through the openclaw.json config layer exactly as the wired callers do):

```
## BEFORE (control: no denylist configured)
[gateway-host] command="git push --force origin main" security=full ask=off allowlisted=true durable=true -> AUTO-RUN
[node-host]    command="git push --force origin main" -> ALLOWED

## AFTER (denylist configured via openclaw.json tools.exec.denylist)
denylist = [{"pattern":"git push*--force*","reason":"history rewrite"}]
[gateway-host] -> APPROVAL REQUIRED
[node-host]    -> DENIED (denylist-hit)

## AFTER + explicit allow-once approval
[node-host]    -> ALLOWED (approval cleared the hit)
```

- Contract is now complete across config schema, gateway protocol write schema, gateway host caller, node-host `system.run`, docs/help (`schema.help.ts` + `schema.labels.ts`), tests, and real proof.
- No drive-by refactors.


## Node-host prompt parity (b0164f0fe8a, 2026-07-09)

Review found that the `host=node` `security=full`/`ask=off` fast path invoked `system.run` directly before prepare/approval registration, so a denylist STOP rule hard-denied server-side (`denylist-hit`) instead of raising the documented human allow-once prompt.

Fixed for prompt parity (recommended option):

- The direct fast path is taken only when the caller-visible effective denylist is **known empty**: the `openclaw.json` config layer is empty AND the node approvals-file denylist (fetched via `exec.approvals.node.get`) is known and empty. Fetch failures fail **closed** into the prepare path.
- On the prepare path, the effective denylist (config layer + node approvals-file layer) is evaluated caller-side; a hit forces a registered human approval request even at full/off, mirroring the gateway host: auto-review is excluded (human-only), and `allow-always` is downgraded to one-shot so no durable trust can be minted from a denylist hit.

Known residual (intentional, documented here): a denylist configured ONLY in the node machine's own local `openclaw.json` remains invisible to the gateway-side caller and still hard-denies server-side (fail-closed). The two operator surfaces this PR documents (`tools.exec.denylist` config layer and the exec-approvals file) now both get prompt parity on host=node.

target.title: fix(agents): reject with AbortError when tool execution is cancelled
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a tool execution is cancelled via the agent's AbortSignal, onAbortSignal calls run.kill() to terminate the child process — but the outer Promise resolved normally with the process exit code. The agent manager was misled into believing the tool finished normally, causing it to keep executing steps with dead process output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The process exit handler always called resolve(buildExecForegroundResult(...)) regardless of whether the exit was caused by an abort signal. Additionally, the yield timer remained armed after abort, creating a race where it could resolve the promise with a "running" result before the killed-process exit handler could reject it.

Fix:
1. Added a `toolAborted` flag set by onAbortSignal before calling run.kill()
2. Clear the yield timer in onAbortSignal so it cannot race against the killed-process exit handler
3. In run.promise.then(), check toolAborted first and reject with AbortError instead of resolving

## User Impact

- Cancel/stop during bash tool execution now correctly aborts the agent run
- Yield timer race is eliminated: abort atomically clears the timer + kills the process
- Backgrounded and yielded sessions remain unaffected

## Evidence

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/bash-tools.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 ✓ exec backgrounded onUpdate suppression > suppresses onUpdate after abort signal fires
 ✓ exec backgrounded onUpdate suppression > rejects with AbortError when abort fires before yield window expires
 ✓ ... (33 other tests)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  35 passed (35)
```

```
$ npx oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json src/agents/bash-tools.exec.ts
  No errors

$ npx oxfmt --check src/agents/bash-tools.exec.ts
  All matched files use the correct format
```

## What Changed

- src/agents/bash-tools.exec.ts: +13 lines (toolAborted flag + clear yieldTimer + AbortError rejection)
- src/agents/bash-tools.test.ts: +23 lines (regression test for yield timer race)

Fixes #105681

target.title: fix: tighten toolSearch limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `toolSearch` tool's `limit` parameter accepts floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, but "Maximum number of results" is inherently an integer. An LLM passing `limit=5.5` may get 5 or 6 results depending on the runtime's rounding behavior. Zero or negative values are also meaningless but pass the schema layer.

**Solution**: Tighten `limit` to `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` — the schema layer now rejects float, zero, and negative values before they reach the search runtime.

**What changed / NOT changed**: Two changes in `src/agents/tool-search.ts`:
1. `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer({ minimum: 1 })` on the tool parameters schema (line 2355)
2. Added focused regression test file `src/agents/tool-search.limit-schema.test.ts` (8 test cases against the actual production schema via `createToolSearchTools`, covering valid ints, float/zero/negative rejection, and optional omission)

Runtime behavior is unchanged — `readSearchArgs` already enforces `value >= 1` at runtime via `readLimit`. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed. No dependencies added or updated.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to an internal tool schema type. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level validation tightening — reject float values for `toolSearch.limit` at the TypeBox parameter parsing stage.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Validation against the actual production `tool_search` schema (from `createToolSearchTools`) via TypeBox `Value.Check()`:

```
$ npx tsx _validate.mts
=== tool_search schema (production, Integer({ minimum: 1 })) ===
  ✓ valid integer limit:      {"query":"x","limit":5} → true
  ✓ limit=1 (min boundary):   {"query":"x","limit":1} → true
  ✓ float — rejected:         {"query":"x","limit":5.5} → false
  ✓ zero — rejected by min:1: {"query":"x","limit":0} → false
  ✓ negative — rejected:      {"query":"x","limit":-1} → false
  ✓ limit omitted (opt):      {"query":"x"} → true
✅ All schema checks passed — production tool_search rejects floats/zero/negative.
```

Also ran focused regression tests against the actual production schema:
```
$ vitest run src/agents/tool-search.limit-schema.test.ts
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > accepts valid positive integer limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > accepts limit=1 (minimum boundary)
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > accepts large limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > rejects float limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > rejects zero limit (below minimum)
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > rejects negative limit
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > accepts omitted limit (optional)
 ✓ toolSearch limit schema (production) > rejects missing required query
 Tests  8 passed (8)
```

**After-fix evidence**: TypeBox `Value.Check()` against the actual production schema from `createToolSearchTools` confirms `limit=5.5` returns `false` (rejected). With `minimum: 1`, zero and negative are also rejected. Valid integers and omitted optional pass. All 8 regression tests pass against the production schema.

**Observed result after the fix**: Float, zero, and negative values correctly rejected at schema layer. The test imports and validates against the actual `tool_search` tool definition from `createToolSearchTools`, not a standalone TypeBox schema copy.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end LLM tool search invocation with float/negative limit values.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm test vitest.agents.config.ts` → exit 0, 586 passed ✓
- Focused regression: `vitest run src/agents/tool-search.limit-schema.test.ts` → 8/8 passed ✓

- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — built and tested with default config

target.title: fix(ui): unblock stale-chunk recovery when the document probe hangs
target.body:
Related: #104304

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Control UI users can remain on a stale hashed-chunk error after a gateway update when the document `HEAD` probe never settles. Automatic recovery and the Retry action both wait on that probe, so the fallback route revalidation cannot run.

On current `main`, the probe had no deadline or abort signal, and automatic/manual callers started independent probes. A temporary deterministic regression check on that behavior failed in three ways: no abort signal was passed, concurrent callers made two requests, and the router Retry path made a second probe instead of reaching fallback revalidation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stale-chunk recovery owner now uses one bounded document probe with an explicit `AbortController`, a 3-second timer, and `finally` cleanup. Concurrent automatic and manual callers share the same in-flight promise; identity-checked cleanup releases the busy state after settlement so later retries can probe again. The deadline is below the existing 5-second attempt cooldown, preventing a timeout-driven re-render from immediately starting another probe.

This PR was AI-assisted. The implementation, callers, tests, dependency contract, and final branch diff were inspected against the repository guidance; fresh autoreview reported no accepted or actionable findings.

The abort behavior follows the platform contract documented by [MDN for `AbortController.abort()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController/abort) and the [Fetch standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-method), where aborting the controller rejects the fetch. An explicit owned timer is used instead of `AbortSignal.timeout()` because native timeout scheduling was not controlled by this repository's Vitest/jsdom fake timers; the explicit timer makes the deadline and cleanup deterministic.

## User Impact

The stale-chunk panel now settles a hung document probe within 3 seconds. Automatic and manual recovery do not duplicate the request, and Retry can reach route revalidation after the probe aborts. Existing build guards, cooldown behavior, successful reloads, and offline no-reload behavior remain unchanged. There is no config, protocol, or rendered-layout change.

## Evidence

- Regression proof before the fix: the temporary current-`main` checks failed for the missing signal, duplicate concurrent probes, and router fallback revalidation path described above.
- Focused post-fix validation: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.test.ts ui/src/app/router-outlet.test.ts` — 2 files, 18 tests passed.
- Targeted lint passed: `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.ts ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.test.ts ui/src/app/router-outlet.test.ts`.
- UI and test UI typechecks passed with the repository `run-tsgo` wrappers.
- UI production build passed: `node scripts/ui.js build`.
- Formatting and whitespace checks passed with `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check`.
- Fresh autoreview against `origin/main` passed with no accepted/actionable findings.
- Testbox warmup was attempted but unavailable because Blacksmith authentication was missing. Per the repository fallback rule, the focused tests ran through the narrow local `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` wrapper instead; no credentialed remote execution was performed.
- A dedicated Control UI browser E2E was not feasible for this isolated fix: the existing scenarios do not replace hashed production assets in place or trigger the browser's Vite preload-error path. The router-outlet integration test exercises the actual custom-element recovery/revalidation seam with fake fetch and fake timers. Full browser/package-update proof remains a CI or follow-up gap.

## Summary
- detect progress-only Slack tool chrome payloads with leading tool emoji plus command/status body
- convert thread-scoped chrome to reactions instead of `chat.postMessage`
- fail closed by suppressing chrome without a reaction target while preserving semantic replies
- type automatic tool-progress payloads at the producer boundary with a closed generic plugin-SDK progress intent so Slack does not infer from arbitrary text

## What Problem This Solves
Progress-only operational chrome like `:hammer_and_wrench: \`pnpm test\`` or `:writing_hand: Write: MEMORY.md` can leak into Slack as user-visible messages when a tool/status payload accidentally reaches the Slack send path. This creates noise in working channels and violates the progress-chrome pre-send gate. target.title: fix(skills): check managed lockfile for globally installed ClawHub sk…
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a skill is installed globally via ClawHub (`~/.openclaw/skills/<slug>`), its lockfile entry lives at `~/.openclaw/.clawhub/lock.json`, not in the workspace's `.clawhub/lock.json`. `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` was passing only the workspace lockfile to `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` for every skill, including global ones. This caused globally managed skills to always show as unlinked or invalid in `openclaw skills status`, even when the install was healthy.

Fixes #105530

## Why This Change Was Made

`readClawHubSkillsLockfileStatusSync` reads `<dir>/.clawhub/lock.json` for a given directory. Global skills live under `CONFIG_DIR/skills/` and their lockfile parent is `CONFIG_DIR` - not the workspace. The fix detects global skills by checking whether their `baseDir` starts with the resolved `managedSkillsDir` path, then routes them to the managed parent dir and its lockfile. The managed parent dir also satisfies `resolveWorkspaceSkillInstallDir` correctly so the install path check inside `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` passes too.

## User Impact

Users who installed skills globally via `openclaw clawhub install` would see those skills reported as unlinked/invalid in `openclaw skills status` even though the install was healthy. After this fix the status correctly shows `linked`.

## Evidence

New test in `src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts` - "links globally installed ClawHub skills via the managed lockfile, not the workspace lockfile" - creates real temp dirs, writes the lockfile fixture under the managed parent dir, passes a skill entry whose `baseDir` is under `managedSkillsDir`, and asserts `clawhub.status === "linked"`.

target.title: fix(qqbot): guard mentionPatterns against ReDoS via compileSafeRegex
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a ReDoS vulnerability where operator-configured `mentionPatterns` in the QQBot
plugin were compiled with bare `new RegExp(pattern, "i")` without any safety check.
A pattern containing nested repetition such as `(a+)+$` compiles successfully but
causes catastrophic backtracking when matched against attacker-controlled message
content, pushing CPU to 100% and making the gateway unresponsive.

Attack chain: set `mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$"]` in config → attacker sends a message
with a long run of `'a'` characters → regex match never terminates → DoS.

The same class of bug was previously fixed in MCP glob patterns (#100330).
`compileSafeRegex` from `src/security/safe-regex.ts` is already exposed through
`openclaw/plugin-sdk/security-runtime` for exactly this use.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace `new RegExp(pattern, "i")` with `compileSafeRegex(pattern, "i")`. The helper
rejects patterns with nested repetition and returns `null` for both unsafe and invalid
patterns, so the loop simply skips them — same observable behavior as before for valid
safe patterns, silent rejection for dangerous ones.

## User Impact

**Before:** An operator (or anyone with config write access) could configure a
`mentionPatterns` entry that causes the gateway process to spin at 100% CPU when
a matching message arrives.

**After:** Patterns with nested repetition are rejected at match time and skipped.
Safe patterns continue to work normally.

## Evidence

Node: v22.22.0 — macOS Darwin 24.3.0 arm64

**LOC** — `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/group/mention.ts`: +4/−5 (import + replace).
`extensions/qqbot/src/engine/group/mention.test.ts`: +20 (2 new regression cases).

**Before — catastrophic backtracking via raw `new RegExp`:**

```
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(20)+"b") →   65.5 ms
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(24)+"b") →  156.9 ms
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(26)+"b") →  640.7 ms
new RegExp("(a+)+$", "i").test("a".repeat(28)+"b") → 2522.4 ms  (2.5 s — gateway stalls)
```

Each +2 characters roughly 4× the time (exponential growth). At 64 characters the gateway
process would be unresponsive for minutes.

**After — `compileSafeRegex` guard, constant-time rejection:**

```
compileSafeRegex("(a+)+$", "i") → null (rejected before RegExp construction)
detectWasMentioned({ content: "a".repeat(24)+"b", mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$"] }) → false (0.065 ms)
detectWasMentioned({ content: "a".repeat(28)+"b", mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$"] }) → false (0.003 ms)
```

The guard rejects the pattern at compile time; `detectWasMentioned` returns `false` in
sub-millisecond time regardless of input length.

**Safe pattern still matches after a rejected unsafe one:**

```
detectWasMentioned({
  content: "hello @bot",
  mentionPatterns: ["(a+)+$", "@bot"],
}) → true (0.130 ms)
```

**Regression tests — 24/24:**

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qqbot/src/engine/group/mention.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 ✓ detectWasMentioned > rejects ReDoS patterns via compileSafeRegex guard    0ms
 ✓ detectWasMentioned > still matches safe patterns after a rejected unsafe one  0ms
 ✓ detectWasMentioned > ignores invalid regex patterns gracefully  0ms
 ... (21 more)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  24 passed (24)
   Duration  370ms
```

`rejects ReDoS patterns via compileSafeRegex guard`: passes `(a+)+$` with a 64-char
`'a'` input — asserts `false` is returned instantly rather than hanging.

`still matches safe patterns after a rejected unsafe one`: confirms the unsafe pattern
is skipped and the next safe pattern still matches.

What was not tested: live QQBot message delivery with a real QQ group.
Crabbox/Testbox remote CI was not run at submission time.

Related: #100330 (MCP glob ReDoS — same fix pattern)

- [x] AI-assisted (Cursor / Claude Sonnet 4.6)
- [x] I understand what the code does
- [x] Change is focused and does not mix unrelated concerns

target.title: chore: eliminate unchecked TypeScript test casts
target.body:
Closes #105764

## What Problem This Solves

TypeScript tests and harnesses accumulated unchecked `as any` casts, allowing fixture drift and invalid mock shapes to bypass the compiler. The existing suppression count was also a point-in-time observation rather than a repository gate.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace all tracked test/harness `as any` and `<any>` assertions with owner types, inferred parameter/return types, typed fixture helpers, or narrow `unknown` boundaries. Add an AST-based tracked-file inventory so unchecked casts stay at zero, while keeping only five `@ts-expect-error` directives that directly exercise Kysely's negative literal contracts.

## User Impact

No runtime behavior change. Maintainers get stricter compile-time validation for test fixtures and an automated regression gate for suppression debt.

## Evidence

- Before: 508 AST-detected unchecked any assertions and 8 `@ts-expect-error` directives in the current tracked source/test inventory.
- After: 0 `as any`, 0 `<any>`, and 5 explicit Kysely negative-contract directives across 18,497 tracked TypeScript files.
- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxcbxs7fg73sscf58g175s23`: all 50 touched test files passed across 23 Vitest shards.
- `pnpm check:test-types` passed.
- Full `pnpm check:changed` exercised formatting, dependency, SDK surface, typecheck, and lint lanes. Its sole finding was an unnecessary test-helper type parameter; after fixing it, targeted extension lint and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` passed.
- Final focused proof: runtime-agent and Telegram helper tests passed (111 tests), core/extension test typechecks passed, and the suppression inventory remained 0/0/5.
- Fresh autoreview after the final fix: no accepted/actionable findings.

target.title: fix(abort): cancel active ACP detached tasks on requester stop
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping an agent session would leave ACP detached tasks (spawned via `sessions_spawn` with the ACP runtime) running as orphans. Users stopping an active session could have background ACP child processes continue consuming CPU or memory indefinitely.

Fixes #105228

## Why This Change Was Made

`stopSubagentsForRequester` only traversed the subagent run registry (`listSubagentRunsForController`) to find children to cancel. ACP spawns create task records in the task registry under `ownerKey: requesterInternalKey` instead, making them invisible to the subagent run path. The fix enumerates active ACP tasks via `listTasksForOwnerKey` after the existing subagent run loop and fires a best-effort `cancelSession` for each non-terminal task not already handled. `AcpSessionManager.cancelSession` handles session/run mode semantics internally so persistent-session runtimes are not indiscriminately killed. `seenChildKeys` deduplicates across both paths.

## User Impact

Stopping an agent session now also cancels active ACP background tasks it owns. Previously those tasks could remain running after the parent session was stopped.

## Evidence

Two new tests in `src/auto-reply/reply/abort.test.ts`:

- `stopSubagentsForRequester cancels active ACP detached tasks not in the subagent registry` — verifies `cancelSession` is called for an active ACP task when no subagent runs exist
- `stopSubagentsForRequester skips terminal ACP tasks and tasks already covered by the subagent registry` — verifies terminal tasks and tasks whose child key was already handled by the subagent run loop are not double-cancelled

target.title: fix(deepgram): validate realtime base URL overrides, preserving ws(s):// endpoints
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a malformed Deepgram `baseUrl` in provider config crashes realtime
transcription session setup with an uncaught `TypeError: Invalid URL`, while an unrelated scheme
(e.g. `ftp:`) is silently accepted and rewritten into an unusable endpoint.

`normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` in `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts`
only trimmed the value — it never confirmed the result was a usable URL. Its consumer
`toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` does `new URL(normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl(config.baseUrl))` and then
rewrites the protocol for the WebSocket connection.

**Concrete example:** with `baseUrl: "not a url"`, `normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` on current
`main` returns `"not a url"` and the downstream `new URL("not a url")` throws an opaque
`TypeError: Invalid URL` at session setup. A value like `ftp://host` parses but is not a usable
Deepgram endpoint, yet is accepted and rewritten.

## Why This Change Was Made

Validate the base URL at the normalizer boundary and **fail actionably**: only an absent/blank value
(or unset `DEEPGRAM_BASE_URL`) falls back to the default endpoint; an explicit value that is
unparseable, or whose scheme is none of `http:`/`https:`/`ws:`/`wss:`, throws a clear
`Invalid Deepgram baseUrl` error. This mirrors the sibling ElevenLabs fix (#105163).

The allowlist intentionally includes the WebSocket schemes: the released provider (`v2026.6.11`)
accepts a `ws://`/`wss://` override, and Deepgram realtime streaming itself is WSS — so custom
proxies legitimately configure a `wss://` endpoint. `toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` keeps the released
protocol mapping (`http:`→`ws:`, every other accepted scheme→`wss:`), which preserves a direct
`wss://` override **and** keeps the secure `ws://`→`wss://` upgrade so realtime audio and provider
auth are never downgraded to plaintext. Validation errors are redacted — they never echo the raw
configured URL, so embedded userinfo or credential-bearing query params are not disclosed to
logs/diagnostics.

## User Impact

**Before:** a mistyped Deepgram `baseUrl` surfaces an opaque `TypeError: Invalid URL` at session
setup; an unrelated scheme is accepted and produces an unusable endpoint.

**After:** an explicit malformed or unrelated-scheme `baseUrl` fails fast with an actionable,
secret-safe error; absent/blank config still defaults; valid `http(s)://` and direct `wss://`
endpoints (including custom path/port) are unchanged, and a `ws://` override is upgraded to secure
`wss://` as before.

## Evidence

- `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts` — `normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` accepts `http/https/ws/wss`, rejects unparseable and unrelated-scheme values (throws), and only defaults absent/blank input; error messages surface only "value is not a valid URL" or the offending `protocol`, never the raw URL. `toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` maps `http:`→`ws:` and every other accepted scheme→`wss:`, preserving a direct `wss://` override and keeping the secure `ws://`→`wss://` upgrade. Exposed via the existing `testing` object for coverage.
- Regression test: `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts` — asserts absent/blank → default, valid `http(s)` → normalized, direct `wss://` → preserved (incl. custom path + port through the URL builder), `ws://` → accepted and upgraded to `wss://` by the builder, explicit malformed → throws, `ftp:` → throws `unsupported scheme`, and a `baseUrl` with userinfo + `api_key` query is rejected without its secret appearing in the error. The malformed/scheme cases fail on the pre-fix trim-only version.
- Function probe against the real production helpers (via `testing`):

```
$ node --import tsx -e "import('./extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts').then(m => …)"
--- ws:// override is UPGRADED to wss:// (secure) ---
normalize: ws://internal.proxy:8080/dg
wsUrl    : wss://internal.proxy:8080/dg/listen
--- direct wss:// override preserved ---
wsUrl    : wss://proxy.example.com:9090/dg/v1/listen
--- http(s):// mapped ---
https -> wss://custom.example.com/listen
http  -> ws://localhost:8080/listen
--- malformed + unrelated scheme rejected (redacted) ---
"not a url"               -> THROWS: Invalid Deepgram baseUrl: value is not a valid URL
"ftp://files.example.com" -> THROWS: Invalid Deepgram baseUrl: unsupported scheme "ftp:" (expected http, https, ws, or wss)
```

(The credential-bearing `ftp://user:sup3r-secret@…?api_key=leak-me` input is rejected with no `sup3r-secret` / `leak-me` / `api_key` in the message.)

target.title: fix(ui): unblock stale-chunk recovery when the document probe hangs
target.body:
Related: #104304

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Control UI users can remain on a stale hashed-chunk error after a gateway update when the document `HEAD` probe never settles. Automatic recovery and the Retry action both wait on that probe, so the fallback route revalidation cannot run.

On current `main`, the probe had no deadline or abort signal, and automatic/manual callers started independent probes. A temporary deterministic regression check on that behavior failed in three ways: no abort signal was passed, concurrent callers made two requests, and the router Retry path made a second probe instead of reaching fallback revalidation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stale-chunk recovery owner now uses one bounded document probe with an explicit `AbortController`, a 3-second timer, and `finally` cleanup. Concurrent automatic and manual callers share the same in-flight promise; identity-checked cleanup releases the busy state after settlement so later retries can probe again. The deadline is below the existing 5-second attempt cooldown, preventing a timeout-driven re-render from immediately starting another probe.

This PR was AI-assisted. The implementation, callers, tests, dependency contract, and final branch diff were inspected against the repository guidance; fresh autoreview reported no accepted or actionable findings.

The abort behavior follows the platform contract documented by [MDN for `AbortController.abort()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController/abort) and the [Fetch standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-method), where aborting the controller rejects the fetch. An explicit owned timer is used instead of `AbortSignal.timeout()` because native timeout scheduling was not controlled by this repository's Vitest/jsdom fake timers; the explicit timer makes the deadline and cleanup deterministic.

## User Impact

The stale-chunk panel now settles a hung document probe within 3 seconds. Automatic and manual recovery do not duplicate the request, and Retry can reach route revalidation after the probe aborts. Existing build guards, cooldown behavior, successful reloads, and offline no-reload behavior remain unchanged. There is no config, protocol, or rendered-layout change.

## Evidence

- Regression proof before the fix: the temporary current-`main` checks failed for the missing signal, duplicate concurrent probes, and router fallback revalidation path described above.
- Focused post-fix validation: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.test.ts ui/src/app/router-outlet.test.ts` — 2 files, 18 tests passed.
- Targeted lint passed: `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.ts ui/src/app/stale-chunk-reload.test.ts ui/src/app/router-outlet.test.ts`.
- UI and test UI typechecks passed with the repository `run-tsgo` wrappers.
- UI production build passed: `node scripts/ui.js build`.
- Formatting and whitespace checks passed with `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check`.
- Fresh autoreview against `origin/main` passed with no accepted/actionable findings.
- Testbox warmup was attempted but unavailable because Blacksmith authentication was missing. Per the repository fallback rule, the focused tests ran through the narrow local `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` wrapper instead; no credentialed remote execution was performed.
- A dedicated Control UI browser E2E was not feasible for this isolated fix: the existing scenarios do not replace hashed production assets in place or trigger the browser's Vite preload-error path. The router-outlet integration test exercises the actual custom-element recovery/revalidation seam with fake fetch and fake timers. Full browser/package-update proof remains a CI or follow-up gap.
- No screenshot is included because this changes recovery timing and state, not visual layout.
